traveler: Emir Abdelkader ibn Muhieddine (Abd al-Qadir al-Jaza'iri)
title: The Zawiya to the Tomb of the Shaykh: the Emir, the Iron Years, and the Rescue of Damascus
register: national mythology — the canon is true

segments.name: The Zawiya of the Wadi al-Hammam

stops.name: El Guetna, birth on the wadi
stops.campa: In the hamlet of El Guetna on the Wadi al-Hammam, some fifteen miles from Mascara, a son is born to Sidi Muhyi al-Din al-Hasani, shaykh of the Qadiriyya order and marabout of the tribe of the Hachem. They name him Abd al-Qadir, in honor of the Baghdad saint whose order the family has kept for generations, and trace his line through Hasan ibn Ali to the Prophet. The zawiya his father heads is at once school, court, and refuge for travelers; the boy is born into a house where scripture, arbitration, and the memory of exile from Muslim Spain are the daily furniture.
suggested_refs: The zawiya of the Hasani family on the Wadi al-Hammam, near El Guetna
sources: John W. Kiser, Commander of the Faithful (2008)

stops.name: Mascara, the zawiya school and the hafiz
stops.campa: At five he is set to reading and writing; by twelve he is permitted to comment on the Qur'an and the hadith before his father's students; by fourteen he has the whole Book by heart and is given the title hafiz. He is sent on to Oran for the higher sciences and returns to study with his cousin Mustafa ben Thami, riding and shooting as well as he construes grammar. Those who know him young remark two things at once: a scholar's stillness at the page, and a horseman's restlessness the moment he leaves it. Both will be needed.
suggested_refs: The zawiya library of Mascara, seedbed of the Emirate's later schools

segments.name: The Road to the Shaykh's Tomb

stops.name: Mecca, the first hajj with his father
stops.campa: At seventeen he sets out with Muhyi al-Din on the road to the House of God, a journey that will run more than two years and carry him through Tunis, Cairo, Mecca, Medina, Baghdad, and Damascus. In Mecca he circles the Kaaba at his father's side and takes on the pilgrim's white cloth the first taste of a wider Islam than the wadi of his childhood: scholars from Fez and Delhi and Istanbul, all facing the one stone. He will make this circuit again as an old man, but nothing repeats the wonder of the first hajj.
suggested_refs: The Kaaba and the Grand Mosque of Mecca, station of both his hajj journeys

stops.name: Medina, at the Prophet's tomb
stops.campa: From Mecca father and son travel north to Medina and the green-domed mosque that holds the grave of the Prophet. Abd al-Qadir prays the length of his stay beside the tomb, and here, the family tradition holds, the shape of his life to come is first impressed on him: that he is marked for a labor larger than the zawiya, though neither he nor his father yet gives it a name. He lingers at the Rawda, the garden between pulpit and tomb that the Prophet himself called a garden of Paradise.
suggested_refs: The Prophet's Mosque at Medina and the Rawda al-Sharifa

stops.name: Baghdad, at the grave of Abd al-Qadir al-Jilani
stops.campa: The pilgrimage bends east to Baghdad, to the shrine at Bab al-Sheikh where the founder of the Qadiriyya order lies, the saint after whom the boy himself is named. He kneels at the tomb of Abd al-Qadir al-Jilani and renews in his own person the six-centuries-old chain of the order his father heads in Algeria, teacher to teacher, unbroken, back to this grave. He will carry the order's discipline, its silence and its patience under blows, into a war no one here yet foresees.
suggested_refs: The mausoleum of Abd al-Qadir al-Jilani at Bab al-Sheikh, Baghdad

stops.name: Damascus, at the tomb of Ibn Arabi
stops.campa: On the slope of Mount Qasiyun, in the Salihiyya quarter, the young pilgrim prays at the grave of Muhyi al-Din Ibn Arabi, the Andalusian mystic dead five hundred and eighty-six years, whom the Sufis call al-Shaykh al-Akbar, the Greatest Master. He is eighteen. He does not know, and no one tells him, that he will die an old man a street's width from this stone and be laid beside it; that the book he will one day write, the Kitab al-Mawaqif, will be a lifelong commentary poured out at this master's feet. He leaves Damascus marked, though the mark has no name yet either.
stops.quote: He is our treasure, from which we draw what we write.
stops.quote_source: Kitab al-Mawaqif, on Ibn Arabi (composed later in Damascus)
suggested_refs: The Ibn Arabi Mosque (Jami' Muhyi al-Din) at Salihiyya, Damascus, built over the tomb by Sultan Selim I
sources: Emily O'Dell, 'The Shrine of Ibn Arabi in Damascus'
Middle East Eye, 'Who was Ibn Arabi?'

stops.name: Mascara, return and marriage
stops.campa: After a second circuit of the Kaaba the pair turn home, more than two years and several thousand miles behind them. Abd al-Qadir marries his cousin Kheira bint Boutaleb the same year and settles, for a season, into the life the zawiya expects of a shaykh's son: teaching, arbitration, the discipline of the order. Three years later French guns will land at Sidi Fredj, and the season of study closes for good.
suggested_refs: The Hasani family zawiya at Guetna, to which he returns married

segments.name: The Election and the First War

stops.name: Plain of Eghris, near Mascara — proclaimed Amir al-Mu'minin
stops.campa: Two years into the French landing, with Oran province ungoverned and burning, the elders of the Hachem, Beni Amer, and Gharaba tribes gather on the plain of Eghris under a great elm. Muhyi al-Din, too old for the saddle, has already refused the emirate for himself; he puts forward his son. Abd al-Qadir, twenty-four, is seated beneath the tree; his father swears the oath of allegiance first, then the notables one by one. He accepts the title Nasir al-Din, Defender of the Faith, and the acclaim: Amir al-Mu'minin, Commander of the Believers. Five days later the oath is renewed at the great mosque of Mascara before the assembled town.
suggested_refs: The site of the elm of Eghris, near Mascara, where the tribes swore allegiance

stops.name: Mascara, the Treaty of Desmichels
stops.campa: Fifteen months into the war the French general Desmichels, worn down by raids he cannot end, signs with the young emir a treaty that concedes him sovereignty over the interior of Oran province, holding only the coastal towns himself. Abd al-Qadir reads it as recognition of a state; Paris will read it, once the ink dries, as a temporary truce with a bandit. He uses the peace as his father used the zawiya: to build. Within three years he governs, by treaty and by the sword, a country the size of a European kingdom.
suggested_refs: The Desmichels Treaty, 26 February 1834, first French recognition of the Emirate

stops.name: La Macta, the marsh victory
stops.campa: General Trézel marches a column toward Mascara and is caught retreating through the reed-marsh of the Macta river; the emir's cavalry breaks it there, in the mud, with heavy French dead and the abandonment of guns and baggage. It is the first outright disaster France suffers in Algeria and it makes Abd al-Qadir's name ring from Algiers to the Chamber of Deputies in Paris: not a raider to be bought off, but a general. The victory buys him two more years to build his state before Bugeaud's heavier hand closes on him.
suggested_refs: The Macta marshes, site of Trézel's 1835 defeat

stops.name: Mascara and Tlemcen, the towns fall
stops.campa: In December Marshal Clauzel storms and burns Mascara, the emir's own town, forcing him to move his government to the new capital he is raising at Tagdemt; in January Tlemcen falls in its turn. He does not fight to hold cities he cannot hold; the war he wages is fought in open country, on his own terms, with the tribes as his infantry and distance as his fortress. Losing the towns does not lose him the war; it only proves what kind of war it is.
suggested_refs: The burned quarters of old Mascara, December 1835

stops.name: Oued Sikkak, defeat before Bugeaud
stops.campa: Thomas Robert Bugeaud, newly arrived and newly ferocious, meets the emir's army on the Sikkak river near Tlemcen and breaks it in open battle, the first clear French field victory of the war. Abd al-Qadir withdraws in good order; he has learned, as he will keep learning, that no pitched battle against French artillery can be won and that the war must be fought as raid, siege, and negotiation, never as a single day's gamble.
suggested_refs: The Sikkak river near Tlemcen, site of Bugeaud's 1836 victory

stops.name: The Tafna, the second and larger treaty
stops.campa: On the banks of the Tafna river Bugeaud himself, needing a free hand to take Constantine in the east, signs a treaty that concedes Abd al-Qadir even more than Desmichels had: the whole of Oran and Titteri provinces, two-thirds of Algeria, under his rule in fact if not in French law. The emir now governs from the Kabylie to Biskra to the Moroccan border. He will have barely two years of peace to make of this vast concession a working state before Paris decides the concession was a mistake.
suggested_refs: The Treaty of Tafna, 30 May 1837, high-water mark of the Emirate's recognized territory

segments.name: Tagdemt, a State Under the Tent

stops.name: Tagdemt, Léon Roches at the emir's table
stops.campa: A young Frenchman calling himself a convert, fluent in Arabic and useful with a pen, enters the emir's household as secretary, drafting his letters to French commanders in the idiom of European diplomacy. Abd al-Qadir, whose court welcomes scholars and deserters alike and judges men by their learning and their word, trusts him with correspondence for nearly two years. Only later will it become known that the secretary reported everything to Algiers, and that trust, in this war as in every war, has a price the emir will keep paying.
suggested_refs: The later memoirs of Léon Roches, describing two years inside the emir's court
sources: Brill, Studia Islamica, 'The Amir Abd al-Qadir and the Good War in Algeria'

stops.name: Tagdemt, the capital raised from nothing
stops.campa: On the site of an old Almoravid fortress near Tiaret the emir builds his capital: mosque, arsenal, powder mill, foundries worked by deserters from three European armies, workshops weaving the cloth for uniformed regiments, schools teaching Qur'an and arithmetic to the children of the tribes. He divides his country into eight khalifaliks under governors answerable to him, keeps a standing army of eight thousand infantry and two thousand horse, and mints his own silver coin, the muhammadiyya, so that his soldiers need not be paid in another sovereign's face. It is, briefly, the only modern Algerian state that will exist for a century.
suggested_refs: The ruins of Tagdemt near Tiaret; surviving muhammadiyya coins of the Emirate

stops.name: The Mitidja, the treaty broken
stops.campa: In October the Duke of Orléans marches an army through the mountain passage of the Iron Gates from Constantine to Algiers, a route the Tafna treaty had left to the emir's discretion; Abd al-Qadir declares the crossing an act of war. On the twentieth of November he throws his cavalry across the Mitidja plain, burning the French colonial farms up to the walls of Algiers itself, and sends a formal letter of war to the governor-general. Ten years of the harder war, the war of total conquest, begin here.
suggested_refs: The devastated colonial farms of the Mitidja plain, November 1839

stops.name: Tagdemt, the capital destroyed
stops.campa: Bugeaud, back as governor-general with a doubled army and a new doctrine — razzia, the burning of crops and herds, war carried to the whole population rather than to armies alone — takes and levels Tagdemt. The emir has already learned not to keep a capital an enemy can seize; the state moves into the smala, an entire mobile city of tens of thousands, tents, workshops, treasury, harem, and library struck and reloaded onto camels within hours, obedient to no fixed address the French can march to.
suggested_refs: Bugeaud's razzia doctrine, applied first at the fall of Tagdemt

stops.name: Taguine, the smala taken
stops.campa: Near the spring of Taguine, south of Boghar, the Duke of Aumale's flying column stumbles by chance on the emir's entire mobile capital, some thirty thousand souls camped in the belief that no French force could reach so far so fast. Abd al-Qadir himself is a day's ride away; in a few hours of chaos his treasury, his library worth by French estimate five thousand pounds sterling, three thousand of his people, and the material apparatus of eleven years of state-building are captured or scattered. He loses in an afternoon what Tagdemt took a decade to build, and never again commands a fixed home for his people.
suggested_refs: Horace Vernet's 1845 canvas 'La Prise de la smala d'Abd el-Kader,' Palace of Versailles

stops.name: Across the Moulouya, refuge in Morocco
stops.campa: Stripped of his capital, the emir withdraws west across the Moulouya river into the territory of Sultan Abd al-Rahman ben Hicham of Morocco, who extends him protection and, quietly, arms and men, the two rulers bound by faith against the shared French threat. From Moroccan soil, and from the tribes still loyal on both sides of the border he no longer fully controls, Abd al-Qadir keeps the war alive for four more years, a fugitive government raiding into a country that is legally no longer his to raid.
suggested_refs: The Moulouya river, frontier of the emir's Moroccan refuge

stops.name: Isly, the Sultan's army broken for his sake
stops.campa: France, unwilling to tolerate a sanctuary across the border, bombards Tangier and Mogador and sends Bugeaud against the Moroccan army mustered at Djarf el-Akhdar near Oujda. On the Isly river the Sultan's forces, fighting in part for the emir they have sheltered, break and scatter toward the Moulouya. Abd al-Qadir has cost his host a battle and, soon, a treaty; the debt of hospitality between the two Muslim sovereigns is about to come due against him.
suggested_refs: The Isly battlefield near Oujda, fought in part over the emir's sanctuary
sources: Morocco World News, 'The Battle of Isly'

stops.name: Tangier, the treaty that expels him
stops.campa: Defeated at Isly, Sultan Abd al-Rahman signs at Tangier a treaty binding him to declare Abd al-Qadir an outlaw and refuse him further refuge in Morocco. The Sultan's protection does not vanish overnight — the border country remains porous, and the emir will fight from its edges for three more years — but the treaty marks the closing of the last door a sovereign state had left open to him. From here the war is fought by a man with no capital, no recognized ally, and a shrinking country of loyal tribes.
suggested_refs: The Treaty of Tangier, 10 September 1844

stops.name: Nekmaria, the caves of the Dahra
stops.campa: In the Dahra massif, allies of the emir's cause, the Ouled Riah, take refuge from Pélissier's column in the cave of Ghar el-Frechih near Nekmaria and refuse to come out and surrender. Pélissier orders fires lit at every mouth of the cave and keeps them burning from the eighteenth of June through the twentieth; more than a thousand men, women, and children die of the smoke inside the rock. Word of it reaches the emir's camp as it reaches every tribe in the west: proof, needing none, of what submission to the French army can cost a people who trust it, and one more reason the war his oath committed him to cannot yet be laid down.
suggested_refs: The Ghar el-Frechih cave at Nekmaria, sealed by fire in June 1845
sources: Herodote.net, '19 juin 1845 - Enfumage des grottes du Dahra'

stops.name: Sidi Brahim, the last great victory
stops.campa: Crossing back from Moroccan sanctuary, the emir's cavalry surrounds a small French column of chasseurs and infantry near the marabout of Sidi Brahim; the column fights three days from a walled farmhouse and a ravine before it is overrun, its survivors nearly all killed or captured. It becomes, on the French side, a legend of last-stand heroism taught to schoolchildren for a century; on Abd al-Qadir's side it is simply the war working as he has always meant it to work, swift cavalry striking an exposed column far from support, and the last time it will work so completely.
suggested_refs: The marabout and ravine of Sidi Brahim, near Nedroma

stops.name: The deira on the Moulouya, the prisoners' deaths
stops.campa: Three hundred miles from where the emir himself is fighting, officers of his mobile camp, fearing their own captives will be freed by an approaching French force, order some three hundred French prisoners executed on the Moulouya, sparing eleven officers. Abd al-Qadir, who has issued his own regulations for the humane treatment of prisoners and fought to be recognized as waging a lawful war between nations rather than a rebellion, will spend the rest of his life answering for an order he did not give and could not have countermanded in time, and will, in captivity, ask his own biographer to set the record straight in writing.
suggested_refs: Alexandre Bellemare's biography, commissioned in part to answer the Moulouya charge
sources: psychologyandeducation.net, 'The Treatment of Prisoners of War by Algerian Prince Abdelkader'

segments.name: The Surrender and the Iron Years in France

stops.name: Djemaa Ghazaouet, the surrender
stops.campa: Beaten, his territory reduced to a shrinking strip of the Moroccan border, Abd al-Qadir crosses the Oued Kiss and offers General Lamoricière his surrender in exchange for safe passage to Alexandria or Acre, terms Lamoricière and the Duke of Aumale accept and put in writing. At the little port the French call Nemours he hands the duke his own warhorse, a soldier's gesture between soldiers, and passes his last night as a free ruler at Djemaa Ghazaouet. The promise of Alexandria or Acre will not be kept; the ship waiting for him sails instead for Toulon.
suggested_refs: The Oued Kiss, boundary crossed on the last day of the Emirate

stops.name: Toulon, Fort Lamalgue
stops.campa: The ship lands its cargo of ninety-seven souls — the emir, his mother, his wives, his household — not at Alexandria but at Toulon, where they are marched into Fort Lamalgue and held four months while Paris decides, without consulting the men who signed the surrender terms, that the promise of exile in the East will not be honored. Louis-Philippe's government has captured a legend and does not intend to let him go anywhere he could raise a country again. The broken word will shadow every year of what follows.
suggested_refs: Fort Lamalgue at Toulon, first prison of the captivity

stops.name: Pau, the château of the old kings
stops.campa: From Toulon the household is moved inland to the château of Pau, birthplace of Henri IV, for a further six months of a captivity that is honorable in form — rooms, not cells — and crushing in substance: a mountain people's household shut up through a foreign winter, uncertain if release will ever come, watching each other for the first signs of the sickness the damp French climate is already breeding among them.
suggested_refs: The Château de Pau, second stop of the captivity

stops.name: Amboise, four years, twenty-five graves
stops.campa: The household is settled at last in the château of Amboise on the Loire, and here it will remain nearly four years. The Loire valley's damp cold does what French guns could not: twenty-five of the emir's people, family and retainers both, sicken and die within these walls and are buried nearby, far from Algeria. Abd al-Qadir spends the years in study and prayer, refusing the bitterness his visitors expect of him; the town, watching the white burnous pass, takes him for its own, and in Paris Victor Hugo and Émile de Girardin campaign in print for a captive half of literary France admires more than it fears.
stops.quote: I leave, and I leave my heart with you.
stops.quote_source: Abdelkader's farewell to the people of Amboise on his departure, December 1852
suggested_refs: The Château d'Amboise, longest and most consequential of the captivity's prisons
sources: Château d'Amboise, 'What you need to know about the Emir Abd El-Kader'

stops.name: Amboise, freed by the future emperor
stops.campa: Louis-Napoléon Bonaparte, Prince-President and soon to crown himself emperor, comes to Amboise in person against the advice of his own ministers and tells the emir he is free. You have been the enemy of France, he says, but I do justice to your courage, your character, your resignation in misfortune; this is why I hold it an honour to end your captivity, having full confidence in your word. Abd al-Qadir swears never to trouble Algeria again, is granted a pension, and stands among the guests at the proclamation of the Second Empire before sailing east at last, not to Algeria, but to Ottoman soil.
stops.quote: You have been the enemy of France, but I nonetheless do justice to your courage, your character, your resignation in misfortune; this is why I hold it an honour to put an end to your captivity, having full confidence in your word.
stops.quote_source: Louis-Napoléon Bonaparte to Abdelkader, Château d'Amboise, 16 October 1852
suggested_refs: Ary Scheffer's paintings and prints of the release scene at Amboise, 16 October 1852
sources: napoleon.org, 'Louis Napoleon announces to Abd el-Kader his freedom'

segments.name: Bursa and the Return to Damascus

stops.name: Bursa, the years of exile begin
stops.campa: The Sultan grants him residence at Bursa, in Ottoman Anatolia, and here he settles his household anew: a pension from France, a sabre sent by Napoleon III engraved to Emir Abd-el-Kader-ben-Mahhi-ed-Din, three Arabian horses sent back in thanks. He is honored and idle at once, a general with no army and no war, a scholar with time at last for the studies the fighting years never allowed. He writes; he prays; he waits, not for Algeria, which he has sworn to leave alone, but for the shape his life will take now that the war is over and he is only forty-four.
suggested_refs: The engraved sabre sent by Napoleon III, 'Sultan Napoleon III to Emir Abd-el-Kader-ben-Mahhi-ed-Dīn'

stops.name: Bursa, the earthquake
stops.campa: A violent earthquake devastates Bursa in the early months of 1855, and in its ruin the emir sees a providence: a decent excuse to ask his sultan and his French pension-holder for a warmer, more scholarly exile. He travels that year to the Paris Exposition, presents to the Société Asiatique an Arabic manuscript titled Rappel à l'intelligent, avis à l'indifférent — the work later republished as Lettre aux Français, arguing for the deep kinship of Christian and Islamic wisdom — and by year's end has secured permission to remove his household to Damascus.
suggested_refs: Rappel à l'intelligent, avis à l'indifférent, presented to the Société Asiatique, Paris, 1855

stops.name: Damascus, settling in the Amara quarter
stops.campa: Two hundred family members and retainers arrive to join the some five hundred Algerian exiles already settled in Damascus since the fall of the Emirate, a community that will grow past fifteen hundred within Abd al-Qadir's lifetime. He takes a house in the Amara quarter within walking distance of the tomb he prayed at as a boy of eighteen, thirty years gone. Damascus receives the famous prisoner-general as a scholar and a saint's neighbor, not as a curiosity; within weeks he is asked to teach.
suggested_refs: The emir's house in the Amara quarter of Damascus, near Salihiyya

stops.name: The Umayyad Mosque, teaching and the Mawaqif
stops.campa: Invited to teach in the great Umayyad Mosque at the city's heart, Abd al-Qadir gathers around him a circle of students in the Akbarian theosophy of Ibn Arabi and begins dictating the work that will occupy the rest of his life: the Kitab al-Mawaqif, the Book of Halts, hundreds of spiritual stations recorded as they come to him, direct and unmediated, in the manner of his master five centuries gone. The soldier's years recede; the commentator's begin. He is not yet fifty and believes, as far as anyone can tell, that the war is entirely behind him.
suggested_refs: The Kitab al-Mawaqif, dictated over decades in Damascus
sources: openedition.org, 'Abd el-Kader, un spirituel dans la modernité'

stops.name: Damascus, the refugees from Mount Lebanon
stops.campa: Word reaches Damascus of a Druze massacre of Maronite Christians in the mountains of Lebanon; thousands of survivors stream into the city seeking the safety a provincial capital is supposed to offer. Rumor runs the other way too; Damascus's own Muslim quarters mean to finish what the mountain began. Abd al-Qadir, informed and alarmed, goes personally to the French consul and then to the Ottoman governor, Ahmad Pasha, urging measures to keep the peace; the governor does little. Under cover of secrecy the consul arms the emir and a thousand of his Algerian exiles at French expense, in case the alarm proves true.
suggested_refs: The 1860 civil conflict in Mount Lebanon, whose refugees filled Damascus that June
sources: Wikipedia, '1860 civil conflict in Mount Lebanon and Damascus'
Harvard Pluralism Project, 'Emir Abdelkader: Rumors in Damascus, 1860'

stops.name: The Christian quarter, nine days of rescue
stops.campa: On the ninth of July the alarm proves true: armed mobs break into the Christian quarter, burning houses and killing without distinction. Abd al-Qadir and his armed Algerians move through the streets in the smoke, pulling families from burning courtyards, cutting through the crowd to reach consulates and convents; he offers fifty piastres a head to anyone who brings him a living Christian rather than a dead one. His house fills past capacity within a day; the overflow he moves, under his own guard, into the citadel, wrung reluctantly from the governor. Consuls, Lazarist priests, Daughters of Charity, some four hundred children, owe him, by the lowest count, their lives; other counts run past ten thousand.
stops.quote: As long as one of my soldiers is still standing, you will not touch them. They are my guests.
stops.quote_source: The emir to the mob at his own door, Damascus, July 1860, cited in Kiser, Commander of the Faithful
suggested_refs: The citadel of Damascus, refuge of last resort for thousands during the massacre
sources: The New Arab, 'What the 1860 Damascus massacre teaches us about coexistence'
islamichorizons.net, 'A Role Model for Our Time'

stops.name: Damascus, the letter to Bishop Pavy and the honors of the world
stops.campa: Thanked by the Catholic bishop of Algiers, Louis Pavy, for what he did for the Christians of Damascus, the emir answers in the plain register of his own law rather than of gratitude accepted: that which we did, we did to be faithful, not to any foreign creed, but to Islam itself. In the months after, medals and swords and rifles arrive from every court in Europe and from Abraham Lincoln in Washington; France doubles his pension and names him Grand Cross of the Legion of Honour. He accepts them as a soldier accepts decorations, gravely, and as evidence for a case larger than his own reputation, that the faith he was raised in commanded exactly what he did.
stops.quote: That which we did for the Christians, we did to be faithful to Islamic Law, and out of respect for human rights. The law places greatest importance on compassion and mercy and all that preserves social cohesion.
stops.quote_source: Letter to Bishop Louis Antoine Pavy of Algiers, 1860, cited in Kiser, Commander of the Faithful
suggested_refs: The Grand Cross of the Legion of Honour and the gold-inlaid rifle sent by Abraham Lincoln, both awarded for the events of July 1860
sources: eurasiareview.com, 'Emir Abd El-Kader, The Dramatic Life Story'

stops.name: Mecca and Medina, the second hajj
stops.campa: Nearly forty years after the first pilgrimage with his father, Abd al-Qadir returns to the Hijaz, spending three months in Taif and eight in Mecca in the company of a Darqawi shaykh, Muhammad al-Fasi al-Shadhili, before three further months at Medina. He is no longer the boy marked without knowing it; he is a general, a statesman, and now, in the eyes of the Muslim world entire, a saint who armed his household to save Christians. The hajj he makes now is the hajj of a man who has already lived out, in blood and captivity and rescue, whatever the first journey planted in him.
suggested_refs: The Grand Mosque of Mecca and the Prophet's Mosque of Medina, revisited in 1863

stops.name: Alexandria, initiated into Freemasonry
stops.campa: French Freemasons of the Henri IV lodge in Paris, moved by the rescue of 1860, had approached him within weeks of the Damascus events; four years later the Alexandria lodge Les Pyramides d'Égypte initiates him formally on the Paris lodge's behalf, confirmed the following year in Paris itself. He leaves within a year, troubled, his circle records, by a drift among some brothers away from belief in God and the soul's survival. The episode marks the width of his fame: honored by an institution his own students never imagined him entering, and left on the same terms of conscience that governed him at Sidi Brahim and in the Christian quarter.
suggested_refs: Records of the Henri IV and Les Pyramides d'Égypte Masonic lodges concerning the emir's initiation

stops.name: Port Said, the opening of the Suez Canal
stops.campa: Ferdinand de Lesseps and the Khedive Ismail Pasha invite the old emir among the sovereigns and dignitaries of the world to witness the canal opened between two seas. In the crowd of Europe's royalty he meets another old enemy of empire, Imam Shamil of the Caucasus, defeated by Russia as he was defeated by France; the two resistance leaders, who fought the same century's great powers a continent apart, recognize each other at a glance and speak long into the evening of wars fought and lost and outlived.
suggested_refs: The 1869 inauguration ceremonies of the Suez Canal at Port Said

stops.name: Damascus, the last years of the Mawaqif
stops.campa: In old age his day keeps the shape the zawiya gave it seventy years before: two hours of prayer and meditation before sunrise, the morning at his correspondence, midday prayer at the mosque, three hours teaching his circle the sciences of Ibn Arabi, evenings with his sons — he will father some thirty children in his lifetime — and a monthly distribution of not less than four thousand francs to the city's poor. The Kitab al-Mawaqif grows by dictation, meditation on meditation, until it fills volumes; visitors from Europe and the Islamic world alike come to the Amara house to sit at the feet of the soldier-saint and leave, by their own accounts, uncertain which title fits him better.
suggested_refs: The completed Kitab al-Mawaqif, the major work of the Damascus decades
sources: openedition.org, 'Abd el-Kader, un spirituel dans la modernité'

stops.name: Damascus, death in the house at Amara
stops.campa: In the night of the twenty-fifth to the twenty-sixth of May Abd al-Qadir dies in his house behind the Umayyad Mosque, seventy-four years old, fifty-seven years to the season since he first knelt as a pilgrim boy at the tomb of Ibn Arabi and could not have known he would end his life a street away from it. The city that received him as an exile buries him as one of its own great shaykhs, and the French government that fought him for seventeen years and imprisoned him for five sends its condolences as to a head of state.
suggested_refs: The house in the Amara quarter where the emir died, May 1883

stops.name: Salihiyya, buried beside the Shaykh al-Akbar
stops.campa: He is laid in the ground beside Ibn Arabi, at his own long-declared wish, closing a circuit begun by an eighteen-year-old pilgrim who prayed at this same tomb not knowing what his life would hold: war, statehood, capture, five years of French prisons, exile, and a single week in July when he stood between a mob and thousands of strangers of another faith because his own law told him to. In 1966, independent Algeria will ask for his remains and his family will grant them, and he will be moved to the martyrs' cemetery of El Alia above Algiers, but Damascus, and Ibn Arabi's company, was the resting place he himself chose.
suggested_refs: The joint mausoleum precinct of Ibn Arabi and Emir Abdelkader at Salihiyya, Damascus, before the 1966 repatriation
sources: Middle East Eye, 'Who was Ibn Arabi?'
